'''''Banksia serrata''''', commonly known as the '''saw banksia''',<ref name="RBGS" /> the '''old man banksia''',<ref name="NP&WS">{{cite web |title=Old man banksia |url=https://www.nationalparks.nsw.gov.au/plants-and-animals/old-man-banksia |publisher=NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service |access-date=17 November 2020}}</ref> the '''saw-tooth banksia''' or the '''red honeysuckle''' and as '''wiriyagan''' by the [[Cadigal]] people, is a species of woody [[shrub]] or tree of the genus ''[[Banksia]]'', in the family [[Proteaceae]]. [[Indigenous (ecology)|Native]] to the east coast of Australia, it is found from [[Queensland]] to [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]] with outlying populations on [[Tasmania]] and [[Flinders Island]]. Commonly growing as a gnarled tree up to 16 m (50 ft) in height, it can be much smaller in more exposed areas. This ''Banksia'' species has wrinkled grey bark, shiny dark green serrated leaves and large yellow or greyish-yellow flower spikes appearing over summer. The flower spikes, or [[inflorescence]]s, turn grey as they age and pollinated flowers develop into large, grey, woody seed pods called [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]].

''B. serrata'' is one of the four original ''Banksia'' species collected by [[Sir Joseph Banks]] in 1770, and one of four species published in 1782 as part of [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger]]'s original [[Species description|description]] of the genus. There are no recognised [[variety (botany)|varieties]], although it is closely related to ''[[Banksia aemula]]''.  Throughout its range, it grows exclusively in sandy soil, and is usually the dominant plant in [[scrubland]] or low [[woodland]]. ''B. serrata'' is [[pollination|pollinated]] by and provides food for a wide array of [[vertebrate]] and [[invertebrate]] animals in the autumn and winter months, and is an important source of food for [[honeyeater]]s. It is a common plant of parks and gardens.

== Description ==
''Banksia serrata'' usually grows as a gnarled and misshapen tree up to 16 m (50 ft) tall, although in some coastal habitats it grows as a shrub of 1–3 m (3–10 ft), and on exposed coastal cliffs it has even been recorded as a [[prostrate shrub]]. As a tree it usually has a single, stout trunk with warty, [[wikt:knobbly|knobbly]] grey bark up to 3 cm (1.2 in) thick. Trunks are often black from past [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfires]], and ooze a red sap when injured. New growth appears in spring, summer and autumn. New [[wikt:branchlet|branchlets]] are hairy, remaining so for two to three years. Leaves are usually crowded together at the upper end of branches, giving the [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] a thin, sparse appearance. The leaves themselves are dark glossy green above and light green below, {{convert|7|to|20|cm|in|abbr=on}}—rarely up to {{convert|26|cm|in|abbr=on}}—long by {{convert|2|to|4|cm|in|abbr=on|1}}—rarely up to {{convert|4.5|cm|in|abbr=on}}—wide, and oblong to [[wikt:obovate|obovate]] (egg-shaped) in shape. The leaf margins are serrated, except near the base, with lobes between {{convert|1|and|3|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} deep.<ref name="George 1981">{{cite journal | last = George | first=Alex S. | year = 1981 | title = The Genus ''Banksia'' L.f. (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Nuytsia (journal)|Nuytsia]] | volume = 3 | issue = 3 | pages = 239–473 [320–22]| issn = 0085-4417| title-link=The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae) | doi=10.58828/nuy00060 | s2cid=196677407 }}</ref><ref name="Taylor 1988">{{cite book | author=Taylor, Anne |author2=Hopper, Stephen | year=1988 | title = The Banksia Atlas (Australian Flora and Fauna Series Number 8) | pages= [https://archive.org/details/banksiaatlas00tayl/page/212 212]–13| location = Canberra, Australian Capital Territory | publisher = Australian Government Publishing Service | isbn = 0-644-07124-9|author2-link=Stephen Hopper }}</ref>

Cylindrical flower spikes, or [[inflorescence]]s, grow from the ends of 1- to 2-year-old branchlets and have leaves at their base. The spikes are generally {{convert|9|to|12|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide with hundreds of individual flowers arising from an upright woody axis. The woody axis is {{convert|7|to|15|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} high and {{convert|0.9|to|1|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The flowers are cream-grey in colour with cream [[Gynoecium#Pistils|styles]]. Old flower spikes develop into "cones" that consist of up to thirty [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] that develop from the flowers that were pollinated. Old withered flower parts remain on the cones, giving them a hairy appearance. Each follicle is oval in shape, wrinkled in texture, covered with fine hair and {{convert|2.5|–|3.5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} long, {{convert|2.0|–|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} thick, and {{convert|1.5|–|2.2|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide.<ref name="George 1981" />

The obovate seed is {{convert|3|–|3.4|cm|in|abbr=on}} long, fairly flattened, has a papery [[Glossary of botanical terms#W|wing]] and weighs around {{convert|77.5|mg|oz|abbr=on|sigfig=2}}. The seed is composed of the obovate seed body (containing the [[Plant embryogenesis|embryonic]] plant), which measures {{convert|1.0|–|1.2|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|0.9|–|1.1|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. One side, termed the outer surface, is pitted and dark brown and the other is brown-black and warty, sparkling slightly. The seeds are separated in the follicle by a sturdy dark brown [[seed separator]], which is about the same shape as the seeds, with a depression where the seed body sits adjacent to it. The first pair of leaves (called ''[[cotyledon]]s'') produced by seedlings are obovate, dull green and measure {{convert|1|–|1.4|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|1|-|1.5|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide. The [[auricle (botany)|auricle]] at the base of the cotyledon leaf is pointed and measures {{convert|0.2|cm|in|abbr=on|2}} long. The [[hypocotyl]] is thick, hairy and red. The cotyledons are linear to lance-shaped with the narrow end towards the base, {{convert|3.5|–|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} long with serrated margins and a v-shaped [[sinus (botany)|sinus]] at the tip.<ref name="George 1981" /> ''Banksia serrata'' closely resembles ''[[Banksia aemula|B. aemula]]'', but the latter can be distinguished by an orange-brown, rather than greyish, trunk, and adult leaves narrower than {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on|1}}. The inflorescences of ''B. serrata'' are generally a duller grey-yellow in colour, have longer (2–3 mm), more [[wikt:fusiform|fusiform]] or cylindrical pollen presenters on the tips of unopened flowers and the follicles are smaller.<ref name="Walters">{{cite web|url=http://asgap.org.au/b-aem.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100923053151/http://asgap.org.au/b-aem.html|archive-date=23 September 2010|title=''Banksia aemula''|last=Walters|first=Brian|date=November 2007|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society|access-date=4 June 2010}}</ref><ref name="PoNSW">{{cite book| last1 = Harden | first1 = Gwen J. | last2 = Hardin | first2 = David W. | last3 = Godden | first3 = Dianne C. | title = Proteaceae of New South Wales | year = 2000 | publisher = UNSW Press | location = Sydney | isbn = 0-86840-302-4|page = 167}}</ref><ref name="Wrigley 1991">{{cite book | last1 = Wrigley | first1 = John | last2 = Fagg | first2 = Murray | title = Banksias, Waratahs and Grevilleas | year = 1991 | publisher = Angus & Robertson | location = Sydney | isbn = 0-207-17277-3|pages =114–15}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Banksia serrata'' was first collected at [[Botany Bay]] on 29 April 1770, by [[Joseph Banks|Sir Joseph Banks]] and [[Daniel Solander]], naturalists on the British vessel ''[[HMS Endeavour]]'' during Lieutenant (later Captain) [[James Cook]]'s [[First voyage of James Cook|first voyage]] to the [[Pacific Ocean]].<ref name="Wharton 1893">{{cite book | editor = William J. L. Wharton | year = 1893 | title = Captain Cook's Journal during his First Voyage Round the World made in H. M. Bark "Endeavour" 1768–71: A Literal Transcription of the Original MSS | location = London | publisher = E. Stock| title-link = Wikisource:Captain Cook's Journal, First Voyage }}</ref><ref name="Banks 1770">{{cite web | author = Banks, Joseph | title = 29 April 1770 | work = Banks's Journal | url = http://southseas.nla.gov.au/journals/banks/17700429.html | access-date = 25 October 2006 | author-link = Joseph Banks| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20061008005340/http://southseas.nla.gov.au/journals/banks/17700429.html| archive-date= 8 October 2006 | url-status= live}}</ref> Solander coined the (unpublished) binomial name ''Leucadendrum serratifolium'', with ''Leucadendron serratum'' also appearing under the finished drawing in ''[[Banks' Florilegium]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Diment |first1=Judith A. |author-link1=Judith Diment |last2=Humphries |first2=Christopher J. |author-link2=Chris Humphries |last3=Newington |first3=Linda |last4=Shaughnessy |first4=Elaine |journal=[[Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History)]] |series=Historical Series |title=Catalogue of the Natural History drawings commissioned by Joseph Banks on the Endeavour Voyage 1768–1771 held in the British Museum (Natural History) : Part 1: Botany: Australia |volume=11 (Complete) |pages=1–183 [149]|publisher=[[British Museum (Natural History)]] |publication-place=London |date=1984 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2355050 |doi=10.5962/p.310430|doi-access=free }}</ref> The first formal [[species description|description]] of the species was not published until April 1782, when [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger]] described the first four ''Banksia'' species in his ''[[Supplementum Plantarum]]'', commenting that it was the showiest species in the genus.<ref name="L.f. 1782">{{cite book | author = Carolus Linnaeus the Younger | year = 1782 | title = Supplementum Plantarum | location = Brunsvigae | publisher = Orphanotrophei|url=http://botanicus.org/page/411159 | page=126| author-link = Carolus Linnaeus the Younger }}</ref> As the first named species of the genus, ''Banksia serrata'' is considered the [[type species]].<ref name="George 1981" /> ''Banksia serrata'' has the common names of old man banksia, saw banksia, saw-toothed banksia and saw-leaved banksia. It is also known as red honeysuckle and red banksia from the colour of its timber.<ref name="Wrigley 1991" /> The Cadigal people who lived in the Sydney region prior to the arrival of Europeans, called the plant wiriyagan.<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Harden |first1=Gwen J. |title=''Banksia serrata'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Banksia~serrata |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney |access-date=11 January 2020}}</ref>

German botanist [[Joseph Gaertner]] described ''Banksia conchifera'' in 1788 in the first volume of his work ''[[De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum]]''.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gaertner|first=Joseph |title=De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum|publisher=Sumtibus Auctoris, Typis Academiae Carolinae|location=Stuttgart|date=1788|volume=1|page=221|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/37174207|language=la}}</ref> Alex George noted this description was taken from Linnaeus' original and was hence a ''[[nomen illegitimum]]'' (illegitimate name).<ref name="George 1981" /> [[Joseph Knight (horticulturist)|Joseph Knight]] described ''Banksia mitis'' and ''Banksia serræfolia'' in his 1809 ''[[On the cultivation of the plants belonging to the natural order of Proteeae]]'', both later determined to be ''B. serrata'' and hence superfluous. In 1830, [[John Lindley]] wrote of a plant in cultivation in England with short wavy leaves in ''[[The Botanical Register|Edwards's Botanical Register]]'', giving it the name ''Banksia undulata'' "wavy-leaved banksia" but conceding it may have been a variety of ''B. serrata''.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Lindley|first=John|date=1830|title=''Banksia undulata''|journal=Edwards's Botanical Register|volume=16|pages=1316|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/238733}}</ref>

Under [[Brown's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|Brown's taxonomic arrangement]], ''B. serrata'' was placed in [[subgenus]] ''[[Banksia verae]]'', the "true banksias", because the inflorescence is a typical ''Banksia'' flower spike. ''Banksia verae'' was renamed ''[[Eubanksia]]'' by [[Stephan Ladislaus Endlicher|Stephan Endlicher]] in 1847, and demoted to [[Section (botany)|sectional]] rank by [[Carl Meissner]] in [[Meissner's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|his 1856 classification]]. Meissner further divided ''Eubanksia'' into four [[Series (botany)|series]], placing ''B. serrata'' in series ''[[Banksia ser. Quercinae|Quercinae]]'' on the basis of its toothed leaves.<ref name="Meissner 1856">{{cite book | last = Meissner | first = Carl | year = 1856 | chapter = Proteaceae | editor-last = de Candolle | editor-first=A. P | editor-link=Augustin Pyramus de Candolle | title = Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis, pars decima quarta | location = Paris | publisher = Sumptibus Victoris Masson | language = la | author-link = Carl Meissner}}</ref> When [[George Bentham]] published [[Bentham's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|his 1870 arrangement]] in ''[[Flora Australiensis]]'', he discarded Meissner's series, replacing them with four [[Section (botany)|sections]]. ''B. serrata'' was placed in ''Orthostylis'', a somewhat heterogeneous section containing 18 species.<ref name="Bentham 1870">{{cite encyclopedia | last = Bentham | first = George | year = 1870 | title = Banksia | encyclopedia = [[Flora Australiensis]]: A Description of the Plants of the Australian Territory | volume = 5: Myoporineae to Proteaceae | pages = 541–62 | location = London | publisher = L. Reeve & Co. | author-link = George Bentham}}</ref>

In 1891, [[Otto Kuntze]], in his ''[[Revisio Generum Plantarum]]'', rejected the generic name ''Banksia'' [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger|L.f.]], on the grounds that the name ''Banksia'' had previously been published in 1776 as ''Banksia'' [[Johann Reinhold Forster|J.R.Forst]] & [[Georg Forster|G.Forst]], referring to the genus now known as ''[[Pimelea]]''. Kuntze proposed ''Sirmuellera'' as an alternative, referring to this species as ''Sirmuellera serrata''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kuntze |first=Otto |authorlink=Otto Kuntze |title=Revisio generum plantarum |volume=2 |publisher=Arthur Felix |location=Leipzig |year=1891 |pages=581–582 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/4004}}</ref> For the same reason, [[James Britten]] transferred the species to the genus ''Isostylis'' as ''Isostylis serrata'' in 1905.<ref name="britten 1905">{{cite book|last=Britten|first=James|author-link=James Britten|title=Illustrations of Australian plants collected in 1770 during Captain Cook's voyage round the world | editor1-first=Joseph | editor2-last=Solander | editor2-first=Daniel C. |publisher=Printed by order of the Trustees of the British Museum|location=London, United Kingdom|year=1905|volume=3 |page=84|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/10165546 |editor-last=Banks | editor-link=Joseph Banks }}</ref> These applications of the [[principle of priority]] were largely ignored,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rehder |first1=A. |authorlink1=Alfred Rehder |last2=Weatherby |first2=C. A. |authorlink2=Charles Alfred Weatherby |last3=Mansfeld |first3=R. |authorlink3=Rudolf Mansfeld |last4=Green |first4=M. L. |authorlink4=Mary Letitia Green |title=Conservation of Later Generic Homonyms |journal=Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew) |year=1935 |volume=1935 |issue=6/9 |page=368 |doi=10.2307/4107078 |jstor=4107078|doi-access=free }}</ref> and ''Banksia'' L.f. was [[conserved name|formally conserved]] and ''Sirmuellera'' rejected in 1940.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sprague |first=T. A. |authorlink=Thomas Archibald Sprague |title=Additional Nomina Generica Conservanda (Pteridophyta and Phanerogamae) |journal=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |year=1940 |volume=1940 |issue=3 |doi=10.2307/4111642 |jstor=4111642 |page=99}}</ref>

=== Current placement ===
[[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]] published a new taxonomic arrangement of ''Banksia'' in his 1981 monograph "[[The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae)]]".<ref name="George 1981" /> Endlicher's ''Eubanksia'' became [[Banksia subg. Banksia|''B.'' subg. ''Banksia'']], and was divided into three sections. ''B. serrata'' was placed in [[Banksia sect. Banksia|''B.'' sect. ''Banksia'']], and this was further divided into nine series, placing ''B. serrata'' in [[Banksia ser. Banksia|''B.'' ser. ''Banksia'']] (formerly ''Orthostylis'').<ref name="George 1999">{{Cite encyclopedia | last = George | first = Alex S. | author-link = Alex George (botanist) | year = 1999 | title = ''Banksia'' | editor = Wilson, Annette | encyclopedia = [[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]] | volume = 17B: Proteaceae 3: Hakea to Dryandra | pages = 175–251 | location = Collingwood, Victoria | publisher = [[CSIRO Publishing]] / [[Australian Biological Resources Study]] | isbn = 0-643-06454-0}}</ref>{{efn|1=George's 1981 publication of ''B.'' ser. ''Orthostylis'' was invalid, as the inclusion of ''B. serrata'', meant that it was required under the [[International Code of Botanical Nomenclature]] to be given the [[autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''Banksia'' L.f. ser. ''Banksia'' . This has been recognised and corrected in later publications.<ref name="George 1999" />}}

In 1996, [[Kevin Thiele]] and [[Pauline Ladiges]] published a new arrangement for the genus, after [[cladistics|cladistic]] analyses yielded a [[cladogram]] significantly different from George's arrangement. [[Thiele and Ladiges' taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|Thiele and Ladiges' arrangement]] retained ''B. serrata'' in series ''Banksia'', placing it in [[Banksia subser. Banksia|''B.'' subser. ''Banksia'']] along with  ''B. aemula'' as its [[sister taxon]] (united by their unusual seedling leaves) and ''B. ornata'' as its next closest relative.<ref name="Thiele 1996">{{cite journal | last1 = Thiele | first1 = Kevin | author-link1 = Kevin Thiele | last2 = Ladiges | first2 = Pauline Y. | author-link2 = Pauline Ladiges | year = 1996 | title = A cladistic analysis of ''Banksia'' (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 9 | issue = 5 | pages = 661–733 | doi = 10.1071/SB9960661 | bibcode = 1996AuSyB...9..661T }}</ref> This arrangement stood until 1999, when George effectively reverted to his 1981 arrangement in his monograph for the ''[[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]]'' series.<ref name="George 1999" />

Under [[George's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|George's taxonomic arrangement of ''Banksia'']], ''B. serrata'' is placed in the [[Genus]] ''[[Banksia]]'', [[Subgenus]] ''[[Banksia subg. Banksia|Banksia]]'', [[Section (botany)|Section]] ''[[Banksia sect. Banksia|Banksia]]'' and [[Series (botany)|Series]] ''[[Banksia ser. Banksia|Banksia]]'' along with ''B. aemula'', ''[[Banksia ornata|B. ornata]]'', ''[[Banksia baxteri|B. baxteri]]'', ''[[Banksia speciosa|B. speciosa]]'', ''[[Banksia menziesii|B. menziesii]]'', ''[[Banksia candolleana|B. candolleana]]'' and ''[[Banksia sceptrum|B. sceptrum]]''.<ref name="George 1999" />

In 2002, a [[molecular phylogenetics|molecular]] study by [[Austin Mast]] again showed that the three eastern species formed a natural group, or [[clade]], but they were only distantly related to other members of the series ''Banksia''. Instead, they formed a sister group to a large group comprising the series [[Banksia ser. Prostratae|Prostratae]], [[Banksia ser. Ochraceae|Ochraceae]], [[Banksia ser. Tetragonae|Tetragonae]] (including ''Banksia elderiana''), ''[[Banksia lullfitzii]]'' and ''[[Banksia baueri]]''.<ref name="Mast 2002">{{cite journal | first1 = Austin R. | last1 = Mast | author-link1 = Austin Mast | last2 = Givnish | first2= Thomas J. | author-link2 = Thomas J. Givnish |date=August 2002 | title = Historical biogeography and the origin of stomatal distributions in ''Banksia'' and ''Dryandra'' (Proteaceae) based on their cpDNA phylogeny | journal = American Journal of Botany | volume = 89 | issue = 8 | pages = 1311–23 | doi = 10.3732/ajb.89.8.1311 | issn = 0002-9122 | pmid=21665734| doi-access = free }}</ref>

In 2005, Mast, Eric Jones and Shawn Havery published the results of their cladistic analyses of [[DNA sequence]] data for ''Banksia''. They inferred a [[phylogeny]] greatly different from the accepted taxonomic arrangement, including finding ''Banksia'' to be [[paraphyly|paraphyletic]] with respect to ''[[Banksia ser. Dryandra|Dryandra]]''.<ref name="Mast 2005">{{cite journal | last1 = Mast | first1 = Austin R. | last2 = Jones | first2 = Eric H. | last3 = Havery | first3 = Shawn P. | year = 2005 | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | title = An assessment of old and new DNA sequence evidence for the paraphyly of ''Banksia'' with respect to ''Dryandra'' (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | pages = 75–88  | doi = 10.1071/SB04015 | bibcode = 2005AuSyB..18...75M }}</ref> A new taxonomic arrangement was not published at the time, but early in 2007 Mast and Thiele initiated a rearrangement by transferring ''Dryandra'' to ''Banksia'', and publishing [[Banksia subg. Spathulatae|''B.'' subg. ''Spathulatae'']] for the species having spoon-shaped [[cotyledon]]s; in this way they also redefined the [[autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''B.'' subg. ''Banksia''. They foreshadowed publishing a full arrangement once DNA [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] of ''Dryandra'' was complete. In the meantime, if Mast and Thiele's nomenclatural changes are taken as an interim arrangement, then ''B. serrata'' is placed in ''B.'' subg. ''Banksia''.<ref name="Mast 2007">{{cite journal | last1 = Mast | first1 = Austin R. | last2 = Thiele | first2 = Kevin | year = 2007 | title = The transfer of ''Dryandra'' R.Br. to ''Banksia'' L.f. (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 20 |issue=1| pages = 63–71 | doi = 10.1071/SB06016 | bibcode = 2007AuSyB..20...63M }}</ref>

=== Intraspecific variation ===
''Banksia serrata'' is a fairly uniform species, showing little variation between different habitats other than occasionally occurring as a shrub in coastal areas. No subspecific taxa are recognised.<ref name="George 1981" /> In 1896, [[Richard Thomas Baker]] found a clump of ''B. serrata'' at Kelgoola on the [[Central Tablelands]] with large leaves, with hairs on leaves and stems, further west of any other collection of the species. He named it ''B. serrata'' var. ''hirsuta''.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Baker |first=Richard Thomas |date=1896|title=On the botany of Rylstone and the Goulburn River districts. Part I|journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales|volume=21|issue=3|pages=427–66 [462]|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/6598773|doi=10.5962/bhl.part.8480|bibcode=1896PLSNS..21..427B |doi-access=free}}</ref> In his 1981 monograph, George was unable to locate a collection that corresponded with the report.<ref name="George 1981" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Banksia serrata'' occurs on the Australian mainland from [[Wilsons Promontory]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] (39°08′ S), in the south, to [[Maryborough, Queensland]] (25°31′ S), in the north.  There is also a large population at [[Sisters Creek, Tasmania|Sisters Creek]] in [[Tasmania]] and another in the southwest corner of the [[Wingaroo Nature Reserve]] in the northern part of [[Flinders Island]]. The Wingaroo NR Conservation Plan (2000) reports that the population comprises around 60 to 80 individual trees, the majority of which are believed to be "quite old". It adds that there is evidence of slow and continuous regeneration, which appears to be occurring in the absence of fire.<ref name="book">{{cite book|last1=George|first1=Alex S.|title=The Banksia book|date=1981|publisher=Kangaroo Press in association with the Society for Growing Australian Plants, NSW | location=Kenthurst, New South Wales |isbn=0-86417-006-8|page=94}}</ref><ref name="tasparks">{{cite web|title=Wingaroo Conservation Area Management Plan 2000|url=http://www.parks.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?id=7099|publisher=Tasmanian Parks and Wildlife Service|access-date=5 June 2017|archive-date=15 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170315211359/http://www.parks.tas.gov.au/file.aspx?id=7099|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Throughout its range, ''B. serrata'' is found on well-drained sandy soils that are low in nutrients, and it is often found on stabilised soil near the coast just behind the main dune system. In the Sydney region it is found with other typical woodland species, including yellow bloodwood (''[[Corymbia eximia]]''), red bloodwood (''[[Corymbia gummifera|C. gummifera]]''), silvertop ash (''[[Eucalyptus sieberi]]''), blue-leaved stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus agglomerata|E. agglomerata]]'') and Sydney peppermint (''[[Eucalyptus piperita|E. piperita]]'').<ref name="Benson" />

In the Upper [[Myall River]] region, ''B. serrata'' grows in dry sclerophyll forest on sandy soils that have recently formed (in the [[Holocene]]) or in shallow soils over differing substrates, while its close relative ''B. aemula'' grows in dry heath forest that occurs on ancient [[Pleistocene]] sands not disturbed in 125,000 years. In intermediate communities both species are found.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Vegetation of beach sand ridges and geomorphological processes in the valley of the Upper Myall River, NSW | journal=Cunninghamia | first1=Peter J. |last1=Myerscough| first2= Roger C. |last2= Carolin | volume=14 | pages=17–53 | year=2014 | doi=10.7751/cunninghamia.2014.14.002}}</ref>

''B. serrata'' is a component of the [[Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub]] (ESBS), designated an endangered ecological community. This community is found on windblown sands, which are younger than the heathlands to the north.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/resources/nature/EECinfoEasternSuburbsBanksiaScrub.pdf|title=Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub in the Sydney Basin Bioregion|date=February 2004|publisher=National Parks and Wildlife Service, New South Wales Government|access-date=8 August 2015}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
{{See also|Ecology of Banksia{{!}}Ecology of ''Banksia''}}
[[File:Calyptorhynchus funereus -Rocky Cape National Park-8.jpg|thumb|[[Yellow-tailed black cockatoo]] at flowers]]
This species is a food source for several bird species. Nectar-eating birds that have been observed feeding at the flowers include [[bell miner]] (''Manorina melanophrys''), [[noisy miner]] (''M. melanocephala''), [[white-cheeked honeyeater]] (''Phylidonyris nigra''), [[New Holland honeyeater]] (''P. novaehollandiae''), [[crescent honeyeater]] (''P. pyrrhopterus''), [[white-eared honeyeater]] (''Nesoptilotis leucotis''), [[brown honeyeater]]  (''Lichmera indistincta''), [[tawny-crowned honeyeater]] (''Gliciphila melanops''), [[white-naped honeyeater]]  (''Melithreptus lunatus''), [[white-plumed honeyeater]]  (''Ptilotula penicillata''), [[yellow-tufted honeyeater]] (''Lichenostomus melanops''), [[eastern spinebill]] (''Acanthorhynchus tenuirostris''), [[red wattlebird]]  (''Anthochaera carunculata''), [[little wattlebird]] (''A. chrysoptera''), [[noisy friarbird]] (''Philemon corniculatus''), [[spangled drongo]] (''Dicrurus bracteatus''), and [[rainbow lorikeet]] (''Trichoglossus moluccanus'').<ref name="Taylor 1988" /><ref name="Benson" /> The immature follicles are eaten by [[yellow-tailed black cockatoo]] (''Zanda funerea'').<ref name="Barker 1984">{{cite book | last1 = Barker | first1 = R.D. | last2 = Vestjens | first2 = W.J.M. | year = 1984 | title = The Food of Australian Birds | publisher = Melbourne University Press |location=Carlton, Victoria | isbn = 0-643-05006-X | pages = '''1''':330, '''2''':197, 232, 458}}</ref>

A 1988 field study found that most flowers of ''B. serrata'' opened at night, and recorded the [[brown antechinus]] (''Antechinus stuartii''), [[sugar glider]] (''Petaurus breviceps''), [[eastern pygmy possum]] (''Cercartetus nanus''), and [[bush rat]] (''Rattus fuscipes'') as nocturnal mammalian visitors and pollinators.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=R. L. |last1=Goldingay |first2= S. M. |last2=Carthew |first3= R. J. |last3=Whelan |title=The Importance of Non-Flying Mammals in Pollination |journal= Oikos |volume= 61 | issue=1 |date=1991 |pages= 79–87 |jstor=3545409 |doi=10.2307/3545409 |bibcode=1991Oikos..61...79G }}</ref> Other mammals recorded eating the flowers include the [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus''), [[little red flying fox]] (''P. scapulatus'') and [[common blossom bat]] (''Syconycteris australis'').<ref name="Benson" /> ''Banksia serrata'' is a host plant for the larval and adult stages of the banksia jewel beetle (''[[Cyrioides imperialis]]'').<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hawkeswood |first=Trevor J. |year=2007 |title=A review of the biology and a new larval host plant for ''Cyrioides imperialis'' (Fabricius, 1801)(Coleoptera: Buprestidae) |journal=Calodema |volume=Supplementary Paper No. 25 |pages=1–3 |url=http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/338.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423181516/http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/338.pdf |archive-date=23 April 2012 }}</ref> Native bees and [[western honey bee|European honey bees]] visit the flowers.<ref name="Taylor 1988" />

''Banksia serrata'' has a central [[taproot]] and few lateral roots. Clusters of fine branched [[Cluster root|proteoid roots]] up to 15 cm (6 in) long arise from larger roots.<ref name=Purnell>{{cite journal|author=Purnell, Helen M.|year=1957|title=Studies of the family Proteaceae. I. Anatomy and morphology of the roots of some Victorian species|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=8|issue=1|pages=38–50|doi=10.1071/BT9600038}}</ref> These roots are particularly efficient at absorbing nutrients from nutrient-poor soils, such as the [[phosphorus]]-deficient native soils of Australia.<ref name="Lamont 1993">{{cite journal |last=Lamont |first=Byron B. | author-link=Byron Lamont | year = 1993 | title = Why are hairy root clusters so abundant in the most nutrient-impoverished soils of Australia | journal = [[Plant and Soil]] | volume = 156 | issue = 1 | pages = 269–72 | doi = 10.1007/BF00025034|bibcode=1993PlSoi.155..269L |s2cid=32550881 }}</ref>

''Banksia serrata'' has shown a variable susceptibility to dieback from the pathogen ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'', the plants in sandier soils showing more resistance than those in heavier soils. Plants from Wilsons Promontory were sensitive. The resistance of plants from Flinders Island is unknown. The small size of the stand renders it vulnerable to eradication.<ref>{{cite book | page=24 | title=Flinders Island Natural Values Survey 2012 | year=2014 | isbn=978-0-9922694-3-2 | author=Natural and Cultural Heritage Division | publisher= Department of Primary Industries, Parks, Water and Environment | location=Hobart, Tasmania | url=https://dpipwe.tas.gov.au/Documents/FlindersIslandReportFULL.pdf}}</ref>

=== Response to fire ===
[[File:Banksia serrata P5270217.jpg|right|thumb|Epicormic regrowth after bushfire]]
''Banksia serrata'' plants generally become fire tolerant by five to seven years of age in that they are able to resprout afterwards.<ref name="Benson">{{cite journal|last1=Benson|first1=Doug|last2=McDougall|first2=Lyn|title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 7b:Dicotyledon families Proteaceae to Rubiaceae|journal=Cunninghamia|date=2000|volume=6|issue=4|pages=1017–1202 [1038]|url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/eea3e2c5-4590-49ce-9114-4b7e8527d491/Volume-6(4)-2000-Cun6Ben1016-1202.pdf.aspx|access-date=16 December 2017|archive-date=28 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228100224/https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/getmedia/eea3e2c5-4590-49ce-9114-4b7e8527d491/Volume-6(4)-2000-Cun6Ben1016-1202.pdf.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> Regrowth is generally from [[epicormic buds]] under their thick bark if the plant is between 2 and 6 m (7–20 ft) high or possibly from the woody subterranean base known as the [[lignotuber]] of younger and smaller plants. There is doubt as to whether recovery from a lignotuber is possible, although it has been demonstrated in other ''Banksia'' species such as ''[[Banksia menziesii|B. menziesii]]''.<ref name="Mibus and Sedgley">{{cite journal|last1=Mibus|first1=Raelene|last2=Sedgley|first2=Margaret|title=Early Lignotuber Formation in ''Banksia'' – Investigations into the Anatomy of the Cotyledonary Node of Two ''Banksia'' (Proteaceae) Species|journal=Annals of Botany|date=2000|volume=86|issue=3|page=577|doi=10.1006/anbo.2000.1219 |bibcode=2000AnBot..86..575M |doi-access=free}}</ref> Stem size is a critical factor; stems with a [[Diameter at breast height|DBH]] of under 1 cm (0.4 in) are unable to withstand low intensity fires. A stem/trunk DBH of 2 cm (0.8 in) is needed to survive low intensity fires and of around 5 cm (2 in) to withstand a high intensity fire.<ref name=bradstock88>{{cite journal |title= The Survival and Population Response to Frequent Fires of Two Woody Resprouters ''Banksia serrata'' and ''Isopogon anemonifolius'' |author1=Bradstock, R.A. |author2=Myerscough, P.J. | journal= Australian Journal of Botany | volume=36|issue=4| pages=415–31 | year=1988 | doi=10.1071/BT9880415 |bibcode=1988AuJB...36..415B }}</ref>

As with other species in the genus, ''B. serrata'' trees are naturally adapted to the presence of regular bushfires and exhibit a form of [[serotiny]] known as [[pyriscence]]. The seedbank in the plant's canopy is released after bushfire. Fire intervals of 10 to 15 years are recommended for the Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub, as longer leads to overgrowth by coastal tea tree (''[[Leptospermum laevigatum]]''),<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/resources/threatenedspecies/0942eastsubsbanksiascrubbpg.pdf |title=Best practice guidelines: Eastern Suburbs Banksia Scrub |page=9 |date=January 2009 |isbn=978-1-74232-091-5|publisher=Department of Environment and Climate Change NSW|location=Sydney, New South Wales |access-date=8 August 2015}}</ref> while an interval of at least nine years was indicated in a study at [[Brisbane Water National Park]].<ref name=bradstock90>{{cite journal |title= Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: ''Banksia serrata'' Lf. and ''Isopogon anemonifolius'' (Salisb.) Knight | author=Bradstock, R.A.| journal= Austral Ecology | volume = 15 |issue = 1| pages = 117–32 | year=1990 | doi=10.1111/j.1442-9993.1990.tb01026.x| bibcode=1990AusEc..15..117B}}</ref> Repeated intervals of five years' duration or less will result in decline of population as young plants are not yet resistant to fire, and their tall [[Habit (biology)|habit]] makes them especially vulnerable.<ref name=bradstock88 /> The seedbank is most productive between 25 and 35 years after a previous fire, although seedlings may be outcompeted by seedlings of [[wikt:obligate#Adjective|obligate]] seeder species.<ref name=bradstock90 /> A field study found that seeds were dispersed up to {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} from the parent plant in an hour by strong wind.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hammill |year=1998|title=Post-fire seed dispersal and species re-establishment in proteaceous heath|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=46|pages=407–19|doi=10.1071/BT96116|first1=K. A.|last2=Bradstock|first2=R. A.|last3=Allaway|first3=W. G.|issue=4 |bibcode=1998AuJB...46..407H }}</ref>

Seeds are also released spontaneously in the absence of fire. The degree to which ''B. serrata'' trees exhibit [[bradyspory]] seems to depend on the nature of the site where they grow. One study recorded plants at coastal sites having more than 30% of their follicles open, compared to those further inland having fewer than 5% open. Follicles also open when part of the tree dies.<ref name="Whelan">{{cite journal|last1=Whelan|first1=R. J.|last2=Jong|first2=N. H.|last3=Burg|first3=S.|title=Variation in bradyspory and seedling recruitment without fire among populations of ''Banksia serrata'' (Proteaceae)|journal=Austral Ecology|date=April 1998|volume=23|issue=2|pages=121–28|doi=10.1111/j.1442-9993.1998.tb00710.x |bibcode=1998AusEc..23..121W }}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[File:Banksia serrata 'Pygmy Possum'.jpg|thumb|right|[[Banksia 'Pygmy Possum'|''Banksia'' 'Pygmy Possum']] at the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Cranbourne]]]]

=== Use in horticulture ===
The gnarled lumpy bark, saw-toothed leaves and silvery-yellow spikes in bud are horticultural features of ''B. serrata''.<ref name="Collins" /> It can be grown readily from seed, collected after heating the "cone". A sterile, free-draining seed-raising mixture prevents [[damping off]].<ref name="seed">{{cite web|title=Growing Banksias from seed|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/banksia/|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=5 June 2017}}</ref> In cultivation, though relatively resistant to ''P. cinnamomi'' dieback, it grows best in a well-drained soil, preferably fairly sandy with a [[pH]] from 5.5 to 7.5, and a sunny aspect.<ref name="Collins">{{cite book |title=Banksias |last1=Collins |first1=Kevin |last2=Collins |first2=Kathy |last3=George | first3=Alex S. |year=2008 |publisher=Bloomings Books Pty Ltd |location=Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=978-1-876473-68-6|pages=328–29}}</ref> Summer watering aids in growth. The plant may take several years to flower, although plants grown from cuttings may flower in two years.<ref name="Collins" /> ''Banksia serrata'' is also used in [[bonsai]].<ref>{{cite web | publisher = Australian National Botanic Gardens | title = Australian Native Plants as Bonsai  | url = https://www.anbg.gov.au/bonsai/ | access-date = 14 November 2006}}</ref>

=== Use in construction ===
Red-pink in colour, the timber resembles English oak.<ref name="Collins" /> It has been used in boatbuilding and is strong, durable and distinctively patterned.<ref name="Wrigley 1991" />

=== Cultivars ===
* [[Banksia 'Pygmy Possum'|''Banksia'' 'Pygmy Possum']] – first propagated by Austraflora Nursery, this is a prostrate form originally from the [[Green Cape, New South Wales|Green Cape]] area on the New South Wales far south coast. Similar plants are seen in nurseries called simply ''B. serrata'' (Prostrate) collected from the same area. This plant is suitable for rockeries and small gardens.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stewart |first=Angus |author-link= Angus Stewart|title=Gardening on the Wild Side |year=2001 |publisher=ABC Books |location=Sydney, New South Wales |isbn=0-7333-0791-4|page=102}}</ref>
* [[Banksia 'Superman'|''Banksia'' 'Superman']] – selection from large-flowered (spikes to {{convert|27|cm|in|abbr=on}} high) and large-leaved population from [[Scotts Head, New South Wales|Scotts Head]] on New South Wales mid north coast. As yet, it is not in commercial cultivation, though is registered with [[Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|ACRA]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc555.html|title=''Banksia'' 'Superman'|last=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority (ACRA)|date=5 August 2002 |work=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=10 June 2017|location=Canberra, Australian Capital Territory}}</ref>
